# Photographing Documentation

Serves Observation and Documentation and Image of the Child

## Why it matters

Most of what children do vanishes in a moment. A tower falls, a puddle dries, and a conversation ends. A photograph keeps a trace of that moment, so we can return to it with the children, with colleagues and with families.

A photo becomes evidence when words travel with it, the children's own and ours. A thoughtful photo shows the competent, capable child we believe in (the image of the child). A careless one can expose a child who cannot yet speak for themselves. This module holds both.

## Three ways in

Choose the way that fits your week. You can do one, two or all three.

- **On my own.** Read the Reading section. Then take five photos of one invitation across a single morning and choose the one that tells the most. Write why in your journal.
- **At a staff meeting.** Bring one photo without its caption. Colleagues say what they see and what they would need to know. Then read your caption aloud.
- **On a PD day.** The full module, hands-on, with a photo walk, a sorting table, and a slide or panel made together.

## Reading

### Why we photograph

Karen Hope, writing in The Sector, asks four questions before any photo is taken.

- Why am I taking this photo, and what is the learning?
- Whose story does it tell?
- Can it help share learning and development with others?
- Is it ethical and respectful of children's rights?

These questions slow us down. A few photos with purpose do more than a full camera roll. One photo with rich language does more than ten with none.

### When photos take over

Karen Hope began her inquiry by asking whether photography in early learning has become excessive. A phone held up all morning can pull an educator out of the moment. The Photography Idea bank card holds one practice for this. The educator's phone stays in a pocket until the children's own noticing is complete.

Kimberley Ainsworth, writing from a Canadian preschool, questioned the habit of treating children's photos as simple windows into their inner thinking. She invites us to see taking a photo as its own event, shaped by the camera, the material and the moment. Every photo we take reflects a choice we made about what to keep inside the frame.

### How we take photos

- **Discreetly.** We take photos without interrupting the children's work, so the moment stays with the child.
- **At the child's level.** We crouch to the child's eye level and the level of their work. A photo taken from above shows the backs of heads.
- **In focus, with important information.** Each photo we keep shows something that matters about the child's experience.
- **About five a week.** A good average is five published photos per child each week.

### Photographing process

A single photo of a finished piece hides the thinking that made it. These ways of looking show the work as it happens (process).

- **Hands at work.** Hands gripping, pouring, sorting, testing and building show effort and intention.
- **A photo series.** Before, during and after, taken from the same spot, shows change over time.
- **The materials up close.** Marks, patterns, arrangements and the traces children leave behind.
- **The space after play.** What children built, gathered or left shows what they chose.
- **The child's view.** Kneel or lie down to see what the child sees.
- **The tries.** Attempts that fell or failed are thinking too, and they belong in the story.
- **Natural light.** Turn off the flash and move toward a window or the open door.

### Faces, identity and belonging

Children seeing themselves helps build a sense of who they are (identity) and of being part of the group (belonging). Inside our community, faces belong. They appear on our walls, in portfolios, in Kaymbu photos to families, in class photo albums and in slides we show.

- Children revisit photos of themselves at their own eye level and add new ideas.
- Family photos, mirrors and self portraits sit beside the photos we take, as in [Seeing Ourselves](tree:pd/26-seeing-ourselves).
- When a photo supports a child's identity or a return to their work (revisiting), we share it with the child.

Outside our community, faces never appear. Anything shown publicly or handed out tells the story through hands, work, posture and setting. A photo without a face can still carry a child's whole experience when we choose the moment with care.

### How children come to understand photos and themselves

Children grow into photos in stages. Knowing these stages helps us choose how we share photos with each age.

- **Around nine months.** Judy DeLoache and colleagues found that babies rub, pat and try to pick objects up off a photograph, even though they can tell a picture from the object. By about nineteen months, pointing at the picture replaces grasping at it. A photo is both an object and a picture of something else (dual representation), and children learn this through experience.
- **Eighteen to twenty-four months.** In Beulah Amsterdam's mirror study, and later work by Michael Lewis and Jeanne Brooks-Gunn, children begin to recognize themselves in a mirror (self-recognition). About half do by eighteen months and most by twenty-four. Tanya Broesch and colleagues found this timing varies across cultures, so it is a pattern and not a rule.
- **Three to four years.** Daniel Povinelli and colleagues showed children a photo taken minutes earlier, with a sticker secretly placed on their heads. Young threes named themselves in the photo but did not reach for the sticker. Older threes and fours did. Connecting "me in the photo" to "me now" (a self that lasts through time) grows across these years.

What this means for us.

- **Twos and threes** hold and point at photos of their class, families and themselves, and name what they see.
- **Threes and fours** begin to connect a photo of yesterday's work to today, so revisiting photos supports memory and a sense of their own story.
- **Fours, fives and TK** can tell the story behind a photo, choose which ones to keep, and decide what a photo should show.

### A child's right to privacy in a digital world

Every child has a right to privacy. Article 16 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child says that no child shall be subjected to arbitrary or unlawful interference with their privacy, family, home or correspondence, or to attacks on their honor and reputation.

In 2021 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child adopted General Comment No. 25, which makes explicit that children's rights apply in the digital environment too. It says privacy is vital to children's agency, dignity and safety, and it names parents sharing photographs online among the risks to it.

Young children cannot agree to having their image shared (consent). They do not yet understand what the internet is, who might see a photo, or how long it lasts. Once a photo is online, we cannot take it back. It can be copied, saved and shared far beyond the people we meant it for.

Stacey Steinberg, a law professor at the University of Florida, calls parents' sharing about their children online "sharenting." She writes that parents now shape a child's digital identity long before the child opens a first email, and that what is shared follows children into adulthood. Her work is about parents, and the same care applies to us. A school holds hundreds of photos of other people's children.

So we hold three commitments.

- **We photograph with purpose.** Each photo serves the child's learning or our community.
- **We share within our community.** Faces stay inside our walls, portfolios, Kaymbu and the slides we show.
- **We decide for the child's future self.** Before sharing, we ask whether this child at sixteen would want this photo out in the world.

### Privacy that grows with the child

Stacey Steinberg notes that a child's interest in privacy develops with age, and that the weight we give a child's own choice should grow with their age and with what is being shared. With our youngest children, we decide for them. As children grow, they ask a friend before taking a photo, choose which photos to print, and say where their work hangs.

### Public-facing photos

Some of our photos leave our community. These include our website, social media, materials for other programs and presentations for outside audiences. Each follows the same care.

- **No faces.** Hands, work, posture and setting tell the story.
- **No names.** Initials only, or no name at all.
- **No locations a stranger could use.** Leave out the school sign in the background and children's names on cubbies or artwork. iNaturalist records use obscured locations.
- **No moments a child might later regret.** Tears, bathroom routines, undressing, conflict and anything a child would want kept private stay out.
- **The director chooses.** Only the director posts or shares photos publicly.
- **Presentations stay on the screen.** Slides with faces are shown and kept with us. Anything handed out shows no faces.

### From photo to evidence

A photo becomes documentation when it carries five things.

- **What a viewer would miss.** The parts that are not obvious from the image.
- **Rich language.** A description that goes beyond what anyone can see.
- **A link.** A context in development or in the project work happening now.
- **The children's language.** Their words, in unaltered quotes.
- **The intention.** The idea behind the work.

From there, the photo joins an observation in TREE. What I noticed holds what happened. What I wonder holds our question. The photo can then become a documentation slide, a panel at children's eye level, or part of a thread.

### Photos in assessment and learning made visible

A photo is one of our strongest pieces of evidence for how a child grows (authentic assessment). NAEYC's position statement on developmentally appropriate practice describes observation, documentation and assessment as ongoing, strategic, reflective and purposeful, woven into the curriculum and daily routines. It also says that, beginning in the preschool years, educators encourage children to use documentation to reflect on their experiences and what they have learned.

Margaret Carr, at the University of Waikato in New Zealand, developed Learning Stories for her country's early childhood curriculum. They are a narrative form of assessment, usually paired with photographs. Gathered over time in a portfolio, they show a child's progress and how educators supported it.

In our program, photos do this work in three ways.

- **Evidence over time.** A photo series of the same child across months shows growth that no single moment can. In TREE, an observation and its photo can count toward up to two DRDP measures, and in the portfolio those measures sit inside the moments, so the assessment stays tied to the experience.
- **Learning made visible.** Panels, slides and the staff room display let children, families and colleagues read the children's thinking.
- **Children's own reflection.** When children revisit photos of their work, they tell us what they were thinking, and their words become new evidence.

A photo is still one moment, seen through our eyes. It shows what happened, and our words and the children's words show why it matters. Assessment rests on many observations over time, read together.

### Whose voice is in the documentation

Margaret Carr designed Learning Stories to hold several voices, the child's, the family's and the educator's. Later studies in New Zealand found those voices are often missing from the finished documentation. A photo with only our caption tells our story. A photo with the child's words and a family's response tells a shared one.

### Children as photographers

Alison Clark and Peter Moss developed the Mosaic approach to listen to young children. In their research, children ages two to four took photos, led tours and made maps of their nursery. Their photos and maps showed adults what mattered most to the children, such as friends, favorite places and feelings.

When children hold the camera, they choose what to keep inside the frame. Children ask a friend before taking a photo of them. The [Photography](tree:ib/photography) Idea bank card holds many ways to begin.

In the Mosaic approach, children and adults first gather material together, such as photos, tours, maps and talk, and then look at it together. Children's photos open a conversation, and the conversation is where adults hear the child's view. Without that conversation, a child's photo is only a picture.

## From our own documentation

Examples from our own observations and documentation appear here once the director chooses them.

## Try this week

Choose one ongoing investigation. Take a photo series of it, before, during and after, and add it to TREE as one observation with the children's words. Ask Karen Hope's four questions before each photo.

The Idea bank cards [Photography](tree:ib/photography) and [Walls and documentation](tree:ib/walls-and-documentation) hold ways to bring this into our day.

## With families

- **Photos with words.** Kaymbu photos carry what a viewer would miss, the children's own words and the intention, so families see why a moment matters.
- **Why our public photos show no faces.** Families know our care for each child's privacy, and that faces stay within our community.
- **Photography at Home.** The family side of the Photography card invites children to photograph what matters to them at home.

## Into our program

- **Class photo albums.** Each class keeps a phone photo album for each child.
- **Kaymbu and TREE.** Photos sent to TREE arrive with their captions and join observations.
- **Documentation slides and walls.** Photos become slides, panels and living documentation, as in [Documentation](tree:pd/02-documentation).
- **Portfolios and conferences.** Photo series show growth over time, with DRDP measures held inside the moments.

## Reflect

- What did your photo series show that one photo would have missed?
- Whose story did your photos tell this week, and whose story was missing?
- Would this child, grown up, be glad this photo exists?

## Share at a staff meeting

Bring one photo without its caption. Ask colleagues what they see, then read your caption and talk about what the words added.

## For the director, sources

- **How we take photos and From photo to evidence.** The photo and documentation guidelines in the Policies and Procedures, as carried in Documentation.
- **Children as photographers.** The Mosaic approach is from Clark and Moss, Listening to Young Children, The Mosaic Approach. The line on what children's photos showed comes from a press summary of that study and is worth checking against the book.
- **Public-facing photos and the age sixteen question.** The director's decisions, November 10, 2026.
- **How children come to understand photos and themselves.** Amsterdam and Lewis and Brooks-Gunn are confirmed through papers that cite them. The nineteen months pointing finding is from an index listing of the DeLoache study and is worth checking against the paper.
- **Whose voice is in the documentation.** The finding that voices are often missing is Cameron's, reported in a New Zealand journal article.

## Presenting this module

**Before the session**

- Choose eight to ten photos from all three classes, some with faces for the internal session and some without for the public-facing practice.
- Print Before you take the photo and Before you share a photo outside our community, one per person.
- Ask each educator to bring one photo from this week without its caption.
- Set out cameras or class phones and an invitation for the photo walk.

| Length | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| 90 minutes | Opening, a photo of you as a child and what it holds for you (10). Hope's four questions (15). Photographing process, a photo walk of one invitation in pairs (25). Faces, identity and privacy, sorting photos into inside our community and public-facing (20). Photo to evidence, captioning a photo with the five things (15). Closing, one commitment (5). |
| Half day | All of the above, plus how children come to understand photos and themselves (20), whose voice is in the documentation with one photo captioned in three voices (20), and a break (15). |
| Full day | All of the above, plus lunch (45), a documentation slide or panel made in pairs from the morning's photo walk (60), photos in assessment by reading a photo series of one child across months (30), and plus and delta (15). |

**During the session**

- Look at the photos with high professional regard. These are colleagues' choices.
- Name the child's right to privacy each time a photo with a face is shown.
- Welcome different readings of the same photo.

**After the session**

- Each educator adds one photo series to TREE this week, as in Try this week.
- Each class checks one public-facing photo against Before you share a photo outside our community.

**PowerPoint.** Every length is presented with a PowerPoint made from this module in TREE's Presenting.

**Internal** uses our own photos from all three classes, with faces.

**External** keeps children's faces and names in the PowerPoint, shown on the screen and kept with us. Anything handed out shows no faces, and every handout names our school. Mark the Presenting entry for outside audiences.
